Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

where $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$: $E_P\varphi=0$ and $E_P\|\varphi\|^2<\infty$. The space $L^2_0(P)$ and its almost-sure equivalence convention are as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $Z_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$ and $R_n=\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)\}-Z_n$. By [F1], $R_n\to0$ in probability. The vectors $\varphi(X_i)$ are iid, centered, and have finite second moment, so [F2] gives $Z_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_k(0,\Sigma_\varphi)$. The covariance is positive semidefinite by $a^T\Sigma_\varphi a=P[(a^T\varphi)^2]\ge0$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^k$.
Fix any $a\in\mathbb R^k$. By [F3], $a^TZ_n\Rightarrow a^TZ$. Also $|a^TR_n|\le\|a\|\|R_n\|$, so $a^TR_n\to0$ in probability. Apply [F4] to obtain $a^T(Z_n+R_n)\Rightarrow a^TZ$.

Step 2.1 holds for every $a$, and $Z$ is the specified Borel Gaussian law from step 1.1. [F5] therefore gives $Z_n+R_n\Rightarrow Z$, which is the asserted limit. No nonsingularity of $\Sigma_\varphi$ is used.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Assume the density-version convention for the path in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. If $s\in L^2(P)$ is a DQM score, then $Ps=0$, so $s\in L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]). Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ are IID real random variables and $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, then, with $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|\longrightarrow0.$$
Consequently $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$

If $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$ on a probability space, then
$\{X,X_0,X_1,\ldots\}$ is uniformly integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $t>0$ let $r_t=\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt{p_0}-\frac t2s\sqrt{p_0}$. On $S^c$, $r_t=\sqrt{p_t}$, so $\alpha_t=\int_{S^c}p_t\,d\mu\le\|r_t\|_2^2=o(t^2)$. Let $B_t=S\cap\{p_t=0\}$. Then $P(B_t)\le\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt{p_0}\|_2^2=O(t^2)$. On $B_t$, the DQM identity gives $\sqrt{p_0}=-\frac t2s\sqrt{p_0}-r_t$, hence $\sqrt{P(B_t)}\le\frac t2\{P[s^2\mathbf1_{B_t}]\}^{1/2}+o(t)$. Since $P(B_t)\to0$ and $s^2$ is integrable, truncating $s^2$ at a fixed bound and then increasing that bound shows $P[s^2\mathbf1_{B_t}]\to0$. Thus $\beta_t:=P(p_t=0)=P(B_t)=o(t^2)$.

For small $t$, $1-\alpha_t>0$. The definition of $q_t$ gives $Pq_t=(1-\alpha_t)^{-1}\int_Sp_t\,d\mu=1$. On $S$, divide the DQM expansion by $\sqrt{p_0}$ and include the normalizer $(1-\alpha_t)^{-1/2}=1+o(t^2)$. With $Y_t=2(\sqrt{q_t}-1)$, this yields $Y_t=ts+R_t$ in $L^2(P)$ with $\|R_t\|_2=o(t)$.

Since $Pq_t=1$ and $q_t=(1+Y_t/2)^2$ $P$-almost surely, linearity [F10] expands this normalization identity to $PY_t=-\frac14P[Y_t^2]$. By [F2], [F3], and step 2.1, $P[Y_t^2]=t^2I+o(t^2)$, so $PY_t=-\frac14t^2I+o(t^2)$.

Suppose $h>0$. By [F4] applied to $s^2$ and [F5] applied to $s(X_i)$, $n^{-1}\sum_i s(X_i)^2\to I$ in probability and $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N(0,I)$. Step 2.1 and [F3] give $E|Y_{t_n}^2-t_n^2s^2|\le\|R_{t_n}\|_2(\|Y_{t_n}\|_2+t_n\|s\|_2)=o(t_n^2)$. Since $nt_n^2=h^2$, linearity [F10] and identical distribution [F6] show that the expected sum of these absolute differences is $o(1)$, so Markov's inequality [F8] makes that sum converge to zero in probability. Also $t_n^2\sum_i s(X_i)^2=(h^2/n)\sum_i s(X_i)^2\to h^2I$ in probability; therefore $\sum_iY_{t_n}(X_i)^2\to h^2I$.

The centered iid sum of $R_{t_n}(X_i)$ has variance at most $n\|R_{t_n}\|_2^2=o(nt_n^2)=o(1)$, so [F8] (applied to its square) gives $\sum_iR_{t_n}(X_i)=nPR_{t_n}+o_P(1)$. By [F2], $PR_{t_n}=PY_{t_n}$; step 3.1 therefore gives $\sum_iY_{t_n}(X_i)=h\Delta_n-\frac14h^2I+o_P(1)$.

The variables $V_n=\sqrt nY_{t_n}(X_1)$ converge in $L^2(P)$ to $hs(X_1)$ by step 2.1. By [F3], $E|V_n^2-h^2s(X_1)^2|\le\|V_n-hs(X_1)\|_2(\|V_n\|_2+h\|s\|_2)\to0$, since the second factor is bounded. Thus [F12] makes $V_n^2$ uniformly integrable. For every $\eta>0$, [F8] and [F9] give $P^{\otimes n}(\max_{i\le n}|Y_{t_n}(X_i)|>\eta)\le\eta^{-2}E[V_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|V_n|>\eta\sqrt n\}}]\to0$, because the tail threshold for $V_n^2$ tends to infinity. Also $P^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\le n\beta_{t_n}=o(1)$ by step 1.1. On the event all factors are positive and $\max_i|Y_{t_n}(X_i)|\le1$, let $g(y)=2\log(1+y/2)$; its third derivative is $g'''(y)=\frac12(1+y/2)^{-3}$, so $|g'''(y)|\le4$ on $[-1,1]$. [F11] gives $g(y)=y-\frac14y^2+O(|y|^3)$ there, with a uniform constant. Thus $\log q_{t_n}(X_i)=Y_{t_n}(X_i)-\frac14Y_{t_n}(X_i)^2+O(|Y_{t_n}(X_i)|^3)$. The sum of cubic terms is bounded by a constant times $\max_i|Y_{t_n}(X_i)|\sum_iY_{t_n}(X_i)^2=o_P(1)$. Steps 3.2–4.1 now yield $\log L_n=h\Delta_n-\frac12h^2I+o_P(1)$.

Decompose $P_{t_n}=(1-\alpha_{t_n})\bar P_{t_n}+\alpha_{t_n}S_{t_n}$, where $\bar P_{t_n}=q_{t_n}P$ and, when $\alpha_{t_n}>0$, $S_{t_n}$ is the normalized restriction to $S^c$. Expanding the product mixture, the all-$\bar P_{t_n}$ term has weight $(1-\alpha_{t_n})^n$ and law $\bar P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}$. If $\alpha_{t_n}>0$, normalize the remaining mixture terms to a probability law $R_{n,t_n}$; then $P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}=(1-\alpha_{t_n})^n\bar P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}+\bigl(1-(1-\alpha_{t_n})^n\bigr)R_{n,t_n}$. When $\alpha_{t_n}=0$, the two product laws are equal. Otherwise, this mixture identity and the event-supremum definition [F7] give $\|P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\le1-(1-\alpha_{t_n})^n\le n\alpha_{t_n}$ by finite subadditivity [F9]. Since $\alpha_{t_n}=o(t_n^2)$ and $nt_n^2=h^2$ for fixed $h>0$, this is $o(1)$. For the asserted product-density identity, the coordinate factors $q_{t_n}$ are nonnegative measurable, so [F14] makes $L_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_iq_{t_n}(x_i)$ product-measurable. Define the measure $Q_n(A)=\int_A L_n\,dP^{\otimes n}$ by [F13]. Repeated Tonelli [F16] on a measurable rectangle $A_1\times\cdots\times A_n$ gives $Q_n(A_1\times\cdots\times A_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n\int_{A_i}q_{t_n}\,dP=\prod_{i=1}^n\bar P_{t_n}(A_i)$, where the one-coordinate identity is the definition $\bar P_{t_n}=q_{t_n}P$. In particular, step 2.1 gives $Q_n(\mathcal X^n)=(Pq_{t_n})^n=1$. By [F15], $\bar P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}$ is also a probability and has the same rectangle values. The measurable rectangles form a pi-system (their intersections are coordinate intersections) generating the finite product sigma-algebra by [F14]; the constant exhaustion $\mathcal X^n$ belongs to it and both measures have mass one there. Thus [F17] proves $Q_n=\bar P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}$ on every product-measurable event. Consequently $L_nP^{\otimes n}=\bar P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}$, identifying exactly the proxy in the statement with the product law compared above. If $h=0$, both product laws equal $P^{\otimes n}$ and $L_n=1$. This proves every assertion.

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

In a local experiment $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ at $h=0$
([[def-lan-experiment]]), let $T_n$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued statistic.
It is **regular at zero with limit law $W$** if, for every fixed
$h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$T_n-h\Rightarrow W\quad\text{under }P_{n,h},$$
where the same probability law $W$ works for all $h$. In a parametric model
with true parameter $\theta_0$, this is the definition for
$T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and local laws at
$\theta_0+h/\sqrt n$; equivalently the centered error
$\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0-h/\sqrt n)$ has a limit independent of
the fixed local displacement $h$.

Assume AC.

Let $P_n$ be probability measures and let $Q_n=L_nP_n$, where $L_n\ge0$ and
$E_{P_n}L_n=1$. Let $T_n$ take values in $\mathbb R^k$. Suppose under $P_n$
that $(T_n,L_n)\Rightarrow(T,e^Z)$, where $Z$ is normal with mean
$-\sigma^2/2$ and variance $\sigma^2$; the joint law of $(T,Z)$ need not be
Gaussian. Then under $Q_n$, $T_n$ converges in distribution to the probability
law determined by
$$E[f(T^{(Q)})]=E[e^Zf(T)]$$
for every bounded continuous $f$. In particular, $Q_n$ is contiguous with
respect to $P_n$. If $(T,Z)$ is jointly Gaussian with
$T\sim N_k(\mu,\Sigma)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(T,Z)=\tau$, this tilted
law is $N_k(\mu+\tau,\Sigma)$, including singular $\Sigma$.
Assume AC. If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\{\mu,\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots\}$ is tight.
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain ([[def-complex-domain]]), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

For a real random variable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, its **characteristic function** is
$$\varphi_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{itX}]=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itx}\,\mathbb P_X(dx),\qquad t\in\mathbb R.$$
For a specified Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$, write $\varphi_\mu(t)=\int e^{itx}\,\mu(dx)$.

The complex integral means the sum of the real integral and $i$ times the imaginary integral, as in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Euler's formula in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] gives $e^{itx}=\cos(tx)+i\sin(tx)$, a continuous function of $x$ with modulus one. Its components are bounded and measurable, hence integrable against a probability measure. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]] therefore applies to this bounded Borel function and proves the displayed identity. [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]] gives $|\varphi_\mu(t)|\le\int1\,d\mu=1$.

No moment assumption is imposed. In particular $X=0$ gives $\varphi_X\equiv1$ and a constant $X=c$ gives $\varphi_X(t)=e^{itc}$. These definitions require no choice of representatives or new use of AC.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Under $P_{n,0}$, $T_n\Rightarrow W$ by regularity at $h=0$ and $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$ by LAN. Marginal tightness gives compact sets with outside probabilities below $\varepsilon/2$; enlarge them to closed balls. Their product is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^{k+d}$ and hence compact by [F11]. By [F12] the joint outside probability is at most $\varepsilon$, so the joint laws of $(T_n,\Delta_n)$ are tight.

By [F4], choose a subsequence along which $(T_n,\Delta_n)\Rightarrow(T,\Delta)$. Its marginals have laws $W$ and $N_d(0,K)$. Fix $h\in\mathbb R^d$. By [F1], $P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$; define $\ell_{n,h}=\log L_{n,h}$ when $L_{n,h}>0$ and $\ell_{n,h}=0$ otherwise. This replacement changes a variable only on an event of probability $o(1)$. For any $a\in\mathbb R^k$ and $b\in\mathbb R$, the projection of $(T_n,\ell_{n,h})$ differs by $o_P(1)$ from $a^TT_n+bh^T\Delta_n-\frac12b h^TKh$. The latter converges by [F7]; applying scalar Slutsky and [F9] to every projection gives $(T_n,\ell_{n,h})\Rightarrow(T,h^T\Delta-\frac12h^TKh)$.

By the continuous mapping theorem [F7], $(T_n,e^{\ell_{n,h}})\Rightarrow(T,e^{h^T\Delta-\frac12h^TKh})$. Since $e^{\ell_{n,h}}=L_{n,h}$ off the event $L_{n,h}=0$, whose probability tends to zero by [F1], the same joint limit holds with $L_{n,h}$. Apply [F3] to this mean-one proxy; [F1] transfers its limit under the proxy law to the actual $P_{n,h}$ law. Regularity and $\delta_n(h)\to Dh$ imply that under this same actual law $T_n\Rightarrow W+Dh$: apply [F7] to each real projection and then [F9]. Therefore for every real $h$ and $t\in\mathbb R^k$, $E[e^{it^TT+h^T\Delta-\frac12h^TKh}]=e^{it^TDh}\varphi_W(t),$ where $\varphi_W(t)=E[e^{it^TW}]$.

Rearranging step 3.1 gives $F_t(h):=E[e^{it^TT+h^T\Delta}]=e^{\frac12h^TKh+it^TDh}\varphi_W(t)$ for every real $h$. For complex $z\in\mathbb C^d$, define $F_t(z)=E[e^{it^TT+z^T\Delta}]$. On every compact set of $z$, its coordinate power series and derivatives are dominated by $e^{R\|\Delta\|_1}$ for some finite $R$, whose expectation is finite because $\Delta$ is Gaussian. Thus $F_t$ is entire in each coordinate, as is the right-hand side. Apply [F5] one coordinate at a time, holding the remaining coordinates real and then extending them successively; the equality holds for every complex $z$.

Put $z=iu$ in step 4.1. By [F13], the resulting characteristic functions satisfy, for all real $t,u$, $E[e^{it^TT+iu^T\Delta}]=\varphi_W(t)e^{-t^TDu-u^TKu/2}.$Set $R=T-DK^{-1}\Delta$ and replace $u$ by $u-K^{-1}D^Tt$. Direct expansion gives$E[e^{it^TR+iu^T\Delta}]=\bigl(\varphi_W(t)e^{t^TDK^{-1}D^Tt/2}\bigr)e^{-u^TKu/2}.$ At $u=0$ the first factor is the characteristic function of $R$; the second is the characteristic function of $\Delta$. The joint characteristic function therefore factors as the product of the marginal characteristic functions.

Let $\rho=\mathcal L(R)\otimes N_d(0,K)$, whose product law exists by [F10]. By [F13], its one-dimensional projection characteristic functions agree with those of $(R,\Delta)$ by step 5.1 and factorization of product integrals. Scalar uniqueness [F8] and [F9] give $\mathcal L(R,\Delta)=\rho$, so $R$ and $\Delta$ are independent. Since $DK^{-1}\Delta\sim N_k(0,DK^{-1}D^T)$ and $T=DK^{-1}\Delta+R$, the law of $T$, which is $W$, is the stated convolution. The argument allows singular $DK^{-1}D^T$ and uses no inverse of that matrix.

Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

where $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$: $E_P\varphi=0$ and $E_P\|\varphi\|^2<\infty$. The space $L^2_0(P)$ and its almost-sure equivalence convention are as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

Assume AC. Let $t\mapsto P_t$ be a one-sided path ($0\le t<\epsilon$) of probability laws on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ dominated by one supplied sigma-finite measure $\mu$, with supplied densities $p_t$ and $P_0=P$. Suppose the path is differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$ with score $s\in L^2(P)$, in the sense of [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. Put $I=P[s^2]$. For a fixed $h\ge0$, let $t_n=h/\sqrt n$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid $P$. On $S=\{p_0>0\}$ set $\alpha_t=P_t(S^c)$ and, for sufficiently small $t$, define

$$q_t(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_t(x)}{(1-\alpha_t)p_0(x)}\quad\text{on }S,\qquad q_t(x)=0\quad\text{on }S^c.$$

Then $q_t$ is a probability density relative to $P$. With $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_{t_n}(X_i)$ and $\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$,

$$\left\|P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV}\longrightarrow0,\qquad \log L_n=h\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^2I+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n\Rightarrow N(0,I).$$

For $h=0$ take $L_n=1$ and use the convention $\log0=-\infty$. The proxy $L_nP^{\otimes n}$ is the normalized absolutely continuous component; the conclusion does not assert a full likelihood ratio for $P_{t_n}^{\otimes n}$.

Assume AC.

Let $P_n$ be probability measures and let $Q_n=L_nP_n$, where $L_n\ge0$ and
$E_{P_n}L_n=1$. Let $T_n$ take values in $\mathbb R^k$. Suppose under $P_n$
that $(T_n,L_n)\Rightarrow(T,e^Z)$, where $Z$ is normal with mean
$-\sigma^2/2$ and variance $\sigma^2$; the joint law of $(T,Z)$ need not be
Gaussian. Then under $Q_n$, $T_n$ converges in distribution to the probability
law determined by
$$E[f(T^{(Q)})]=E[e^Zf(T)]$$
for every bounded continuous $f$. In particular, $Q_n$ is contiguous with
respect to $P_n$. If $(T,Z)$ is jointly Gaussian with
$T\sim N_k(\mu,\Sigma)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(T,Z)=\tau$, this tilted
law is $N_k(\mu+\tau,\Sigma)$, including singular $\Sigma$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let $(X_n)$ and $(Y_n)$ be real random variables on one probability space, and let $X$ be a real random variable (possibly on another space). If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\to c$ in probability for $c\in\mathbb R$, then $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$ and $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$. If $c\ne0$, define $Q_n=X_n/Y_n$ on $\{Y_n\ne0\}$ and give $Q_n$ any fixed value on $\{Y_n=0\}$. Then $Q_n\Rightarrow X/c$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, let $k<\infty$, and let $\widehat\psi_n$ estimate $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$. If it is asymptotically linear at $P$ with influence function $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$, then

$$\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)\}\Rightarrow N_k(0,\Sigma_\varphi),\qquad \Sigma_\varphi=P[\varphi\varphi^T].$$

The covariance may be singular. This is a distributional limit only; the theorem asserts neither local regularity nor estimator attainment of an efficiency bound.

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be a closed linear subspace, and let $\dot\psi:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous linear with an ambient representer $\phi_0\in H^k$, meaning $\dot\psi(s)=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H$ coordinatewise for all $s\in\mathcal T$. Assume Countable Choice. Then all ambient representers are exactly

$$\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k.$$

The unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$ is $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$; when $\dot\psi$ is a statistical path derivative, this is its canonical gradient. Projection is applied coordinatewise.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix an allowed path with score $s$ and a fixed $h>0$. Let $T_n=\sqrt n\{\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)\}$, $\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_i s(X_i)$, and $L_n$ be the proxy ratio from [F3]. By [F3], $P(L_n=0)\to0$; set $\ell_n=\log L_n$ when $L_n>0$ and $\ell_n=0$ otherwise. For arbitrary $a\in\mathbb R^k$ and $b\in\mathbb R$, asymptotic linearity and [F3] give $a^TT_n+b\ell_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\{a^T\varphi(X_i)+bh s(X_i)\}-\tfrac12bh^2P[s^2]+o_P(1).$ The summands are iid and square-integrable by [F1] and [F2].

Apply [F5] to each scalar linear combination in step 1.1, then apply [F6] to its $o_P(1)$ remainder. Since this holds for every $(a,b)$, [F7] gives the joint Gaussian limit of $(T_n,\ell_n)$, with first marginal $N_k(0,\Sigma_\varphi)$ and cross-covariance between $T_n$ and $\ell_n$ equal to $hP[\varphi s]$.

The log-ratio marginal in step 2.1 is $N(-h^2P[s^2]/2,h^2P[s^2])$. Exponentiating the finite version $\ell_n$ by [F7] gives the joint likelihood-ratio limit, and replacing $e^{\ell_n}$ by $L_n$ changes it only on the $o(1)$-probability zero event from step 1.1. Apply [F4] to the proxy law in [F3]; under that law, $T_n\Rightarrow N_k(hP[\varphi s],\Sigma_\varphi)$. Total-variation closeness in [F3] transfers the same limit to the actual law $P_{h/\sqrt n}^{\otimes n}$.

By pathwise differentiability, $\sqrt n\{\psi(P_{h/\sqrt n})-\psi(P)\}\to h\dot\psi_P(s)$. The regularity hypothesis therefore makes $T_n$ under the actual local law converge to $N_k(h\dot\psi_P(s),\Sigma_\varphi)$, using the base limit [F8]. Comparing with step 3.1, uniqueness of weak limits gives $N_k(hP[\varphi s],\Sigma_\varphi)=N_k(h\dot\psi_P(s),\Sigma_\varphi)$. Equal-covariance Gaussian laws have equal means, so $P[\varphi s]=\dot\psi_P(s)$.

Step 4.1 holds for every allowed score. By linearity it holds on their linear span; by [F10] the pairing with $\varphi$ is continuous, and by [F2] the derivative is continuous, so equality extends to the closure $\mathcal T$. Thus $\varphi$ is an ambient representer of the pathwise derivative.

By [F9], $r=\varphi-\phi_{\rm can}$ has every coordinate in $\mathcal T^\perp$. Hence $P[\phi_{\rm can}r^T]=0=P[r\phi_{\rm can}^T]$, and expansion gives $P[\varphi\varphi^T]-V_{\rm can}=P[rr^T]$. For every $a\in\mathbb R^k$, $a^TP[rr^T]a=P[(a^Tr)^2]\ge0$, proving positive-semidefinite dominance.

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $\mathcal T\subseteq H$ be a closed linear subspace, and let $\dot\psi:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous linear with an ambient representer $\phi_0\in H^k$, meaning $\dot\psi(s)=\langle\phi_0,s\rangle_H$ coordinatewise for all $s\in\mathcal T$. Assume Countable Choice. Then all ambient representers are exactly

$$\phi_0+(\mathcal T^\perp)^k.$$

The unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$ is $\phi_{\mathrm{can}}=\Pi_{\mathcal T}\phi_0$; when $\dot\psi$ is a statistical path derivative, this is its canonical gradient. Projection is applied coordinatewise.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

In a local experiment $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ at $h=0$
([[def-lan-experiment]]), let $T_n$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued statistic.
It is **regular at zero with limit law $W$** if, for every fixed
$h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$T_n-h\Rightarrow W\quad\text{under }P_{n,h},$$
where the same probability law $W$ works for all $h$. In a parametric model
with true parameter $\theta_0$, this is the definition for
$T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and local laws at
$\theta_0+h/\sqrt n$; equivalently the centered error
$\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0-h/\sqrt n)$ has a limit independent of
the fixed local displacement $h$.

Assume AC and let $d,k\ge1$ be finite. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be LAN at $h=0$ with positive-definite information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$. Let $\psi_{n,h}\in\mathbb R^k$ be a local target such that for every fixed $h$,

$$\delta_n(h):=\sqrt n(\psi_{n,h}-\psi_{n,0})\longrightarrow Dh$$

for a fixed matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}$. Suppose $T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\psi_n-\psi_{n,0})$ is regular for this target: under each fixed $P_{n,h}$, $T_n-\delta_n(h)\Rightarrow W$ for the same Borel law $W$. Then there is a probability law $\nu$ on $\mathbb R^k$ such that

$$\mathcal L(W)=N_k(0,DK^{-1}D^T)*\nu.$$

The Gaussian covariance may be singular. No finite-moment hypothesis on $W$ or $\nu$ is needed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For any $a\in\mathbb R^k$, the projection of $a^T\phi_{\rm can}$ onto $\mathcal S$ is $a^TDI^{-1}S$: its residual has inner product $a^TD-a^TDI^{-1}P[SS^T]=0$ with every linear combination of the score coordinates. Therefore the covariance matrix of the projected gradient is $DI^{-1}D^T$.

By [F2] and [[thm-qmd-implies-lan-for-iid]], this finite-dimensional submodel has the required LAN proxy and total-variation control. The regularity premise in the statement and [F4] give $L\stackrel d=G_\gamma+W_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma\sim N_k(0,DI^{-1}D^T)$ is independent of $W_\gamma$. Since $L$ has finite covariance and $G_\gamma$ does, $W_\gamma$ has finite covariance as well; independence yields $\operatorname{Cov}(L)=DI^{-1}D^T+\operatorname{Cov}(W_\gamma)\succeq DI^{-1}D^T$.

If $\mathcal T=\{0\}$, then $\phi_{\rm can}=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(L)\succeq0=V_{\rm can}$. Otherwise fix $a\in\mathbb R^k$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Density of the union of the $\mathcal S_\gamma$ in $\mathcal T$ provides an index $\gamma$ and $g\in\mathcal S_\gamma$ with $\|g-a^T\phi_{\rm can}\|_{L^2(P)}<\varepsilon$. The projection formula in step 1.1 is orthogonal, so for any $g\in\mathcal S_\gamma$, $\|a^T\phi_{\rm can}-g\|_2^2=\|a^T\phi_{\rm can}-\Pi_{\mathcal S_\gamma}(a^T\phi_{\rm can})\|_2^2+\|\Pi_{\mathcal S_\gamma}(a^T\phi_{\rm can})-g\|_2^2$. Thus the projection error is below $\varepsilon$, and the quadratic forms $a^TD_\gamma I_\gamma^{-1}D_\gamma^Ta$ approach $a^TV_{\rm can}a$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

When $\mathcal T\ne\{0\}$, step 2.1 gives $a^T\operatorname{Cov}(L)a\ge a^TD_\gamma I_\gamma^{-1}D_\gamma^Ta$ for every $\gamma$. Take the approximation in step 2.2 with arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$ to obtain $a^T\operatorname{Cov}(L)a\ge a^TV_{\rm can}a$. Since this holds for every $a$, $\operatorname{Cov}(L)\succeq V_{\rm can}$. Together with the zero-tangent case in step 2.2, this proves the claim.

[F12] with $n=1$ gives $\sqrt{1+ts}=1+\frac t2s+O(t^2\|s\|_\infty^2)$ uniformly. The remainder is $o(t)$ in $L^2(P)$, so this is a DQM path with score $s$. Its mean is $\psi(P_{t,s})=\mu+tP[Xs]$, hence $\dot\psi_P(s)=P[(X-\mu)s]$.

Bounded centered functions are dense in $L^2_0(P)$: for $g\in L^2_0(P)$, the bounded functions $g_M=g\mathbf1_{\{|g|\le M\}}-P[g\mathbf1_{\{|g|\le M\}}]$ are centered and converge to $g$ in $L^2(P)$ by truncation and $Pg=0$. Thus $\mathcal T=L^2_0(P)$. By [F10], $\dot\psi_P$ is continuous and is represented by $\phi=X-\mu\in\mathcal T$; [F9] makes this the canonical gradient. Its covariance is $V_{\rm can}=P[(X-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2$.
The identity $\bar X_n-\mu=(P_n-P)(X-\mu)$ proves exact asymptotic linearity with influence $\varphi=X-\mu$. Therefore [F7] gives the base limit $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

Fix a bounded centered score $s$ and $h\ge0$. Under the base law, the iid vectors $(X_i-\mu,s(X_i))$ have finite second moment. By [F4], their normalized sums converge jointly to a centered Gaussian with covariance entries $\sigma^2$, $P[(X-\mu)s]$, and $P[s^2]$. The lemma [F5] also gives $P(L_n=0)\to0$; set $\ell_n=\log L_n$ when $L_n>0$ and $\ell_n=0$ otherwise, which changes the joint law only on an $o(1)$-probability event. Scalar Slutsky and Cramér–Wold [F11] give the joint Gaussian limit with $\ell_n$; exponentiation gives the likelihood-ratio limit required by [F6]. The proxy limit of $\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)$ is therefore $N(hP[(X-\mu)s],\sigma^2)$, and total-variation closeness [F5] transfers it to the actual local law.

The target shift is exact: $\sqrt n\{\psi(P_{h/\sqrt n,s})-\mu\}=hP[(X-\mu)s]$. Subtracting it from step 1.4 gives $N(0,\sigma^2)$ for every fixed $h\ge0$, so the sample mean is regular on every allowed path. Its influence covariance is $\sigma^2=V_{\rm can}$ by step 1.2; [F8] shows it attains the regular asymptotically linear lower bound. This includes $\sigma^2=0$, when both covariance matrices vanish.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Let $P$ be a probability law for one observation, let $\mathcal P$ be a model of laws containing $P$, and let $\psi:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^k$ be a target functional, where $k\ge1$ is finite. A one-sided path $t\mapsto P_t$, $0\le t<\epsilon$, through $P=P_0$ is **differentiable in quadratic mean (DQM)** with score $s\in L^2(P)$ when its densities $p_t,p$ relative to one common sigma-finite measure $\mu$ satisfy

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

The score initially belongs to $L^2(P)$; [[thm-dqm-score-mean-zero]] proves it is unique modulo $P$-almost-sure equality and has mean zero, so it lies in $L^2_0(P)$ as defined by [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. The allowed scores form the **tangent set** of the designated paths ([[def-tangent-set]]); their **tangent space** $\mathcal T$ is the closure of their real linear span in $L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-tangent-space]]). It is a closed linear subspace by [[thm-tangent-space-is-closed-linear-subspace]], and hence a Hilbert space under Countable Choice ([[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]).

The functional $\psi$ is **pathwise differentiable at $P$ relative to $\mathcal T$** if the right derivative $\dot\psi_P(s):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(\psi(P_t)-\psi(P))/t$ exists for every allowed path, depends only on its score, and extends to a continuous linear map $\dot\psi_P:\mathcal T\to\mathbb R^k$. A vector $\phi\in L^2_0(P)^k$ is a **parameter influence curve** (or representer) when

$$\dot\psi_P(s)=E_P[\phi s]\qquad(s\in\mathcal T),$$

with the expectation interpreted coordinatewise. The Hilbert-space Riesz theorem gives a unique representer in $\mathcal T^k$; it is the **canonical gradient**. This representation requires Countable Choice, as in [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] and [[def-countable-choice]]. The supplied density versions along a path use the separate Axiom of Choice in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. The full set of ambient representers and its projection characterization are proved in [[thm-influence-curve-representers]].

derivations.claim: The masses sum to one. The geometric series gives $Pf=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j/2}<\infty$, while $P[f^2]=\sum_{j\ge1}1=\infty$. Thus $\mu=Pf$ is finite and $u=f-\mu$ is integrable, centered, but not square-integrable.

For any bounded centered $s$, choose $t\ge0$ so small that $|ts|\le1/2$ everywhere. Then $1+ts\ge0$ and $P(1+ts)=1$. On $[-1/2,1/2]$, $g(x)=\sqrt{1+x}$ has $g''(x)=-1/(4(1+x)^{3/2})$, so $|g''(x)|\le1$. [F4] with $n=1$ gives $\sqrt{1+ts}=1+\frac t2s+O(t^2\|s\|_\infty^2)$ uniformly; thus the tilt is DQM with score $s$. Since $f\in L^1(P)$ and $s$ is bounded, $\psi(P_{t,s})=Pf+tP[fs]$ and $\dot\psi_P(s)=P[us]$.

For $M>0$, put $u_M=u\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le M\}}$, $c_M=Pu_M$, and $s_M=u_M-c_M$. Then $s_M$ is bounded and centered, $D_M:=P[u^2\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le M\}}]=P[us_M]$, and $\|s_M\|_2^2=D_M-c_M^2\le D_M$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $u(j)\ge2^{j/2}/2$, so each such included atom contributes at least $1/4$ to $D_M$; as $M\to\infty$, arbitrarily many atoms are included and $D_M\to\infty$. For large $M$, $s_M\ne0$ because the truncation vanishes on a positive-mass tail and is nonzero on included atoms. Hence $|\dot\psi_P(s_M)|/\|s_M\|_2\ge\sqrt{D_M}\to\infty$.

If a finite-variance influence curve $\phi\in L^2_0(P)$ represented these derivatives, [F3] would give $|\dot\psi_P(s_M)|=|P[\phi s_M]|\le\|\phi\|_2\|s_M\|_2$ for every $M$, contradicting step 1.3. Thus the mean functional has no square-integrable influence curve in this model, refuting the statement.
